title: End of Year Value Booster: the Led Tasso
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart describes a role-play activity he calls "Bizarro Stu" (a play on Ted Lasso's "Led Tasso" persona-swap), used once or twice a semester to give students practice articulating why their schoolwork matters. The teacher performs a despairing, nihilistic persona — "it's garbage, it's pointless" — and challenges small groups to argue him out of it within a time limit, tracking and pressure-testing their arguments on the board before finally conceding. He frames the exercise as a variant of Strategy 6 ("Valued Within") from The Will to Learn, useful because it trains students to construct value-arguments themselves rather than simply receiving the teacher's. He recommends it specifically for the end of the year, since students will need exactly this skill — defending the worth of hard work to a skeptic — for the rest of their lives, whether or not a teacher is there to prompt them. It's a short, concrete script teachers can lift and run in a single class period.
points: Provides a ready-to-run script (the "Bizarro Stu" persona-swap) rather than an abstract principle, making it directly usable without adaptation.
Frames the activity's value as building students' own capacity to argue for the worth of hard work, not just absorbing the teacher's pitch — a shift from teacher-generated to student-generated Value.
Recommends timing it for the end of the year specifically, positioning it as a transferable life skill rather than a classroom-only exercise.
Notes the format doubles as teacher enjoyment and renewal, an explicit acknowledgment that sustainable classroom practices need to work for the teacher too.
quotes: On most days, you and I need to be the folks in the room who are rock solid in our grasp of why the work of learning in our class matters. If we don't know the Value of the work, we can't expect our students to.
Students, I've had it. I can no longer see why the work we do in here is worthwhile. In fact, I'm convinced it's not. It's garbage. It's pointless. It's done nothing for you.

I mean, think about it: when are you ever going to need to read literature in real life? To write essays? To take notes on new material? To engage in pop-up debates? These are not real-world activities — they are contrived, cutesy school things.

This is great for the end of the school year because it gives your students practice at what they'll need to do for the rest of their lives: figure out why the work of learning is valuable, even when that Value has its skeptics, even when the person in charge has lost their way.
Group your students into fours and give the groups three minutes to come up with the best arguments they can muster. At the end of the time, each group nominates a speaker to make their best case.
